abstract: In natural human–AI dialogue, users’ corrections, requests, and self-descriptions carry reusable signals about how they want work to be done. These signals reveal individual process preferences, user-specific standards for evidence, depth, analytical focus, procedure, and delivery. We ask whether a preference revealed in one dialogue can shape an assistant’s later answer when the task does not restate it. ProcessPrefBench uses three months of natural dialogues from two knowledge workers to build 66 source–target cases separately judged for source evidence and target applicability. Sources are preselected, so the benchmark tests application rather than retrieval. We test three models with target-only, full-history, and distilled-preference prompts. Target-specific 0–2 rubrics score preference realization, and a task gate flags severe failures. Compared with target-only prompting, full-history and imperative distilled-preference prompting raise preference realization by 0.204 and 0.244 points on the 0–2 scale, respectively, with no reliable advantage from distillation. Fabricated-evidence failures rise from 5.8% under target-only prompting to 10.1% under full-history and 10.4% under imperative prompting. ProcessPrefBench highlights a tension in learning from dialogue, where drawing on prior interactions can improve preference realization yet also invite fabricated evidence. We hope it helps build assistants that honor a user’s process preferences without sacrificing factual reliability.

sections.body: The paper defines individual process preferences as reusable, user-specific standards for how work should be done, such as what evidence supports a claim, how an analysis is organized, and whether a deliverable needs confirmation. It frames learning these from dialogue as a delayed, cross-task problem with three possible failures: the system preserves the wrong standard, fails to realize a correct one, or imports remembered content as unsupported target claims. ProcessPrefBench studies a narrower setting where the relevant source dialogue is preselected for each target, so it tests application rather than retrieval. Figure 1 shows a case where an April correction is not restated six weeks later.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Users reveal process preferences in dialogue, and ProcessPrefBench tests whether an assistant applies one learned in an earlier dialogue to a new task.

sections.body: Long-term-memory benchmarks such as LoCoMo, LongMemEval, and MemoryAgentBench test whether information stays available across extended interactions. Personalization benchmarks, including PersonaMem, LaMP, PrefEval, CUPID, and AlpsBench, usually supply the user signal more directly. Closer work such as PRELUDE and TRACE learns preferences from edits or corrections, but the paper's focus is tracing a source-supported standard into a different task and separating functional realization from surface mention. External memory systems, including mem0, store and reintroduce information, and HaluMem studies hallucinations introduced by memory operations. The authors argue retrieval alone neither ensures transfer nor blocks carried-over content from entering target claims.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Existing benchmarks test either memory of dialogue or stated preferences, not whether a preference induced from dialogue transfers to a new task.

sections.body: Data come from three months of natural interactions by two knowledge workers using Margin. Each user annotates their own traces; a source is kept only when the user's words support a reusable standard through correction, prescription, or self-description, and factual repairs, current-task requests, and scene-bound conclusions are excluded. The same owner then judges a separate same-user target that does not repeat the preference but should improve with the standard. Each case has one to three source-anchored atoms scored not applicable, 0, 1, or 2, where 2 requires a functional change to reasoning, organization, conclusion, or delivery. A separate task gate flags severe failures, including fabricated evidence, which is labeled operationally when target-side materials do not support specific claims. For 13 cases with truncated reading context, verified source material was restored.
sections.heading: Benchmark Construction
sections.headline: Each case pairs a source dialogue supporting a reusable standard with a same-user target that does not restate it.

sections.body: Every condition shares the system prompt, page context, and verbatim user question. Target-only prompting adds no memory, full-history prompting adds the complete source interaction, and the distilled conditions add a distilled preference, applied always (imperative) or only when relevant (conditional). The mem0 external-memory system is also tested. The models are DeepSeek V4 Flash, Qwen-Max, and GPT-4o, and each case is generated twice. Claude Sonnet 4.6 serves as the preference and task-gate judge in isolated roles, casting three evidence-citing votes per atom and two votes for the gate. On 30 audited answers, human agreement was substantial, with kappa of .72 on preference atoms and .84 on the task gate, while agreement with the judge was lower. Primary comparisons use exact sign tests and cluster-bootstrap intervals; conditional prompting is descriptive.
sections.heading: Evaluation
sections.headline: Three models are tested under target-only, full-history, and distilled-preference prompts, with 1980 answers generated in total.

sections.body: Table 1 reports preference scores and task-failure rates for three models. Imperative distilled-preference prompting exceeds target-only prompting by 0.244 points (95% CI [0.177,0.313]; 48/8/9 wins/ties/losses; exact sign p<.0001), and full-history prompting gains 0.204 points. Distillation does not show a reliable advantage over full history: the difference is +0.026 (95% CI [-0.034,+0.087]; p=.451), and the authors state this does not establish equivalence. Fabricated-evidence failures rise from 5.8% under target-only prompting to 10.4% under imperative prompting (difference 4.5 points; p=.006) and to 10.1% under full-history prompting. Overall task failure rises from 15.2% to 18.9%, not conventionally significant (McNemar p=.086). Sensitivity analyses in Appendix C keep the imperative gain positive.
sections.heading: Results
sections.headline: Full-history and imperative distilled-preference prompts raise preference scores over target-only prompting, but imperative prompting also raises fabricated-evidence failures.

sections.body: The conclusion states that natural dialogue carries evidence of how a user wants work done, and ProcessPrefBench turns that evidence into 66 cross-task cases. Across three models, relevant history improves preference realization. The authors argue the failures are separable: a system may preserve the wrong standard, fail to realize a correctly preserved one, or import remembered content as unsupported claims. They conclude that reliable transfer requires more than retrieving or summarizing a relevant interaction. The benchmark is presented as a way to make progress toward this measurable.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: Relevant history improves preference realization, but preserving the right standard and avoiding imported content remain separate requirements.

sections.body: The benchmark rests on two knowledge workers using one product, with an imbalanced 52/14 case split concentrated in research, sensemaking, and decision tasks. The 66 cases draw on 30 corrective sources and 59 distinct targets, so bootstrap intervals capture within-benchmark variation rather than population uncertainty; source- and target-cluster analyses preserve the main direction. Because each case supplies its relevant source, the test covers cross-task application, not retrieval from heterogeneous histories. The judge audit covers 30 answers from 10 target groups and is diagnostic: it does not validate the between-condition fabrication contrast, and the non-expert annotator scores domain-knowledge answers systematically higher. Headline effects should be read as effects under the benchmark judge.
sections.heading: Limitations
sections.headline: The benchmark rests on two users and 66 cases, and the judge audit is diagnostic, so effects hold under the benchmark judge.

sections.body: The corpus contains natural interaction traces from a user who is also an author and from an independent user. The authors state that inclusion in the corpus does not constitute release permission. Before releasing any material, they plan to confirm participant consent and review each item for privacy, provenance, and redistribution rights. They also state that gated access does not replace de-identification.
sections.heading: Ethics and Privacy
sections.headline: Natural interaction traces are not released until participant consent, privacy, provenance, and redistribution rights are reviewed.

sections.body: The public GitHub repository for the benchmark includes the benchmark definition, construction and evaluation protocols, a public case schema, a synthetic demonstration case, a data card, privacy documentation, licensing and citation metadata, and a release validator. The frozen prompts, evaluation and aggregation code, and de-identified per-answer audit records are being prepared and must first be reviewed for private paths, provenance, and content. Natural interaction cases will be released only after the ethics review. Raw histories, identity mappings, private URLs or paths, consent records, and internal answer keys will not be distributed.
sections.heading: Data and Code Availability
sections.headline: A public repository holds the benchmark definition, protocols, and schema now, while prompts, code, and case data await review.

sections.body: The appendix covers the scoring protocol for preference atoms and the task gate, and human calibration of the judges, including Table 2 agreement figures and the limits of the subtype labels. It then gives sensitivity analyses (Table 3) for the imperative comparisons across users, excluded inversions, source and target clusters, and normal terminations. Appendix D audits two cases end to end: a transfer failure in which all three models compressed the April standard into a neighboring credibility standard, and a successful transfer of a reusable judgment framework. Appendix E gives two fabricated-evidence examples, one from imperative prompting and one from full-history prompting.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix lists the scoring protocol, judge calibration, sensitivity analyses, two end-to-end case audits, and fabricated-evidence examples.
